lessons.title: Classes, objects & references
lessons.summary: Blueprints, new, reference variables, null and ==.

blocks.text: A **class** describes what its objects hold (**fields**) and what they can do (**methods**). It is a blueprint, not a thing.

blocks.caption: Fields are declared up front, with types

blocks.title: Python vs Java
blocks.text: No `__init__` needed to create fields and no `self` parameter. Fields are declared in the class body with a type. Inside a method, `name` simply means this object's field.
`new Dog()` creates an **object** (an instance) and gives back a **reference** to it. The variable `d` stores that reference, not the object itself.

blocks.caption: Prints: Rex woofs

items: Fields get **default values**: `0` for numbers, `false` for boolean, `null` for references.
**Local variables** get no default. Reading one before assigning it does not compile.

steps.prompt: Create a Dog and set its name.
steps.explanation: `new` creates the object. Fields are accessed with the dot operator: `d.name`. Java has no `self`, and `create` is not a keyword.

steps.prompt: What is the output?
options: An exception is thrown at runtime
steps.explanation: Fields are always initialized: `int` to `0`, references to `null`, `boolean` to `false`. Concatenating `null` into a String prints the text `null`. Only **local** variables lack defaults.

blocks.text: Assigning one reference variable to another copies the **reference**, not the object. Both variables now point to the same object.

blocks.title: Python vs Java
blocks.text: Same as Python: `b = a` makes two names for one object. Nothing is copied.
Assigning a **new** object to `b` later only moves `b`. `a` still points to the old object.

steps.prompt: What is the output?
steps.explanation: `b = a` makes both point to the first Cup, so `a.ml = 100` sets it. Then `b = new Cup()` moves only `b` to a second Cup, which gets 200. `a` is unaffected.

blocks.text: A reference can be `null`: it points to **no object**. Using a field or method through a `null` reference compiles fine but throws a **NullPointerException** (NPE) at runtime.

blocks.code:
Dog d = null;
d.bark();   // compiles, then NPE

blocks.title: Compiles, then crashes
blocks.text: The compiler does not track null. `Dog d = null; d.bark();` compiles. The failure happens only when the line runs.

steps.prompt: Tap the line that throws an exception at runtime.
steps.explanation: Line 6 prints `null` (the field's default value). Line 7 reads a field through the `null` reference `q`, which throws NullPointerException.

blocks.text: For objects, `==` asks **is it the same object?** It compares references. `equals()` asks **do they mean the same value?** — but only if the class defines it.

blocks.caption: Prints false, then true

items: `String` overrides `equals()` to compare characters.
Your own class without an `equals()` override inherits the version from `Object`, which behaves like `==`.
Printing an object without a `toString()` override gives something like `Dog@1b6d3586` (class name + hash). You'll write `toString()` to get readable output.

blocks.title: Python vs Java
blocks.text: Python `==` calls `__eq__` (value), and `is` checks identity. In Java, `==` on objects is like Python `is`.

steps.prompt: What is the output?
steps.explanation: `t1` and `t2` are different objects, so `==` is false. `Tag` doesn't override `equals()`, so it falls back to identity: also false, even though both hold "a". `t3` points to the same object as `t1`, so `t1 == t3` is true.

steps.prompt: Which two statements are true? Choose two.
options: A reference variable stores the object itself.
Several reference variables can point to the same object.
Calling a method through a null reference throws a NullPointerException.
An instance field of type String defaults to "".
Local variables default to 0 or null like fields do.
steps.explanation: A variable holds a **reference** to the object, so many variables can share one object. Fields of reference type default to `null`, not `""`. Local variables have no default at all; using one unassigned does not compile.

lessons.title: Object life cycle & GC
lessons.summary: When objects become eligible for garbage collection.

blocks.text: Objects live on the **heap**. You never delete them yourself. The **garbage collector** (GC) reclaims objects that the program can no longer reach.
An object is **eligible for GC** when no reference chain from live code (local variables of running methods, static fields) leads to it.

blocks.title: Python vs Java
blocks.text: Python has `del` and reference counting. Java has neither. The rule to remember: **unreachable = eligible**.

steps.title: Three ways to lose an object

items: Set the last reference to `null`.
Reassign the last reference to another object.
The last reference was a local variable and its method returned.

blocks.code:
Obj a = new Obj();  // object #1
Obj b = new Obj();  // object #2
a = b;     // #1 unreachable: eligible
b = null;  // #2 still reachable via a

blocks.title: Draw it
blocks.text: On paper, draw each object as a box and each variable as an arrow. Cross out arrows as lines run. Boxes with no arrows from a live variable are eligible.

steps.prompt: How many objects are eligible for garbage collection when line 6 is reached?
steps.explanation: Object #1 is referenced by `a` and `c`. Setting `a = null` still leaves `c`. Then `b = c` drops the only reference to object #2, so exactly **one** object is eligible.

blocks.text: Objects that reference **each other** but are not reachable from live code are still eligible. Java does not count references; it checks reachability.

blocks.title: Referenced ≠ reachable
blocks.text: An object being referenced is not enough. The reference has to come from something reachable. A cycle that nothing reaches is an island, and the whole island is eligible.

steps.prompt: How many Node objects are eligible for garbage collection when line 9 is reached?
steps.explanation: `c` still points to node #3. Following `next`: #3 → #1 → #2. Every node is reachable through `c`, so **none** is eligible. It would be an island only if `c` were also set to null.

blocks.text: A local variable disappears when its method returns. The object it pointed to becomes eligible **unless** a reference escaped: it was returned, or stored in a field.

steps.prompt: After the call `make();` on line 10 finishes, how many objects created inside make() are eligible for GC?
steps.explanation: Three objects are created. The one from `a` is only referenced by a local, so it's eligible after the method returns. The one from `b` is kept by the static field `keep`. The returned object is ignored by the caller (`make();` discards it), so it's eligible too: **2**.

items: `System.gc()` is only a **request**. The JVM may ignore it. You can't force collection.
You can't predict **when** an eligible object is collected, or whether it is collected at all before the program ends.
`finalize()` is deprecated and not on the exam. Never rely on it.

blocks.title: On the exam
blocks.text: Exam questions ask how many objects are **eligible** at a given line. Never answer "when is it collected" with a specific moment: the answer is always "it can't be known".

steps.prompt: Calling `System.gc()` guarantees that all eligible objects are destroyed before the next line runs.
steps.explanation: `System.gc()` only suggests that the JVM run the garbage collector. Nothing is guaranteed: not when, not which objects, not whether it runs at all.

steps.prompt: Which two statements about garbage collection are true? Choose two.
options: An object becomes eligible when no live code can reach it.
Setting a reference to null immediately frees the object's memory.
Two objects that only reference each other can be eligible.
System.gc() forces the garbage collector to run.
An object stored in a static field is eligible when the method that created it returns.
steps.explanation: Eligibility is about reachability, so an isolated cycle is eligible. `null` only removes a reference; actual collection happens later, if ever. `System.gc()` is a hint. A static field keeps its object reachable for as long as the class is loaded.

steps.prompt: Tap the line after which the object created on line 1 first becomes eligible for GC.
steps.explanation: Track object #1: line 1 `p`, line 2 also `q`. Line 3 moves `p` away, but `q` remains. Line 4 adds `r`. Line 5 drops `q`, but `r` remains. Line 6 moves `r` to object #2, removing the last reference to #1.

lessons.title: Instance vs static members
lessons.summary: Shared static fields, static methods and static imports.

steps.title: One per object, or one per class

blocks.text: An **instance field** exists once per object. A **static field** exists once per **class**, shared by every object.

blocks.caption: Prints: 2 1 3

blocks.title: Python vs Java
blocks.text: Close to a Python class attribute. But in Python, `self.total += 1` creates a new instance attribute. In Java, `a.total++` always updates the one shared static field.

steps.prompt: What is the output?
steps.explanation: `next` is static and shared. `t1.issue()` sets id 1 (next becomes 2), `t2.issue()` sets id 2 (next 3), then `t1.issue()` again sets t1's id to 3 (next 4). `next++` returns the old value.

blocks.text: A **static method** belongs to the class, not to an object. So there is no `this` inside it.

items: A static method **can** use other static fields and methods directly.
It **cannot** use instance fields or instance methods directly — which object's would it use?
It can use them through an object: `new Shop().sell()`.
An instance method can use **both** static and instance members.

blocks.title: Why main is special
blocks.text: `main` is static. That's why calling an instance method from `main` without an object fails to compile.

steps.prompt: Tap the line that does not compile.
steps.explanation: `info()` is static, so it has no object and cannot read the instance field `stock`. Line 10 is fine: an instance method may call a static method.

blocks.text: You can call a static member through a reference variable. The compiler only looks at the variable's **declared type**; the object is never used.

blocks.caption: Prints hi — no NullPointerException

blocks.title: null, but no NPE
blocks.text: A static call through a `null` reference does **not** throw an NPE. The exam loves this. Good style is `Util.hi()`, but the reference version compiles.

steps.prompt: What is the output?
options: An exception is thrown at runtime
steps.explanation: `add()` and `count` are static, so `lamp.add()` and `lamp.count++` really mean `Lamp.add()` and `Lamp.count++`. The `null` value of `lamp` is never used, so there is no exception. `count` goes 0 → 1 → 2.

blocks.text: A **static import** lets you use static members without the class name.

blocks.title: Word order
blocks.text: The syntax is `import static`. Writing `static import` does not compile. You import **members** (`Math.max`), not just the class.

steps.prompt: Complete the static import so the code prints 7.
steps.explanation: `import static java.lang.Math.max;` imports the static method `max`, so it can be called without `Math.`. The order is `import static`, never `static import`.

steps.prompt: Which two lines compile when inserted at // INSERT? Choose two.
steps.explanation: `main` is static, so it can't use the instance field `x`, the instance method `go()`, or `this`. It can use the static field `y` directly and call `go()` through a new object.

steps.prompt: A static method may use `this` as long as it is called through an object reference.
steps.explanation: A static method never has a `this`, however it is called. `obj.staticMethod()` is compiled as `ClassName.staticMethod()`. Using `this` in a static method is always a compile error.

lessons.title: Constructors
lessons.summary: Default and overloaded constructors, this(...) and final fields.

blocks.text: A **constructor** runs when `new` creates an object. It has the **same name as the class** and **no return type**, not even `void`.
`this.name` is the field; plain `name` is the parameter.

blocks.title: Python vs Java
blocks.text: Like `__init__`, but named after the class, without `self`. A class may have **several** constructors with different parameters.
If you write **no** constructor, the compiler adds a no-argument one for you: the **default constructor**.

blocks.title: It disappears
blocks.text: As soon as you declare **any** constructor, the default one is gone. `new Dog()` then fails to compile unless you write `Dog() { }` yourself.

steps.prompt: Tap the line that does not compile.
steps.explanation: `Cat` declares a constructor, so the compiler does not add a default no-arg one. `new Cat()` has no matching constructor.

blocks.text: A class can have several constructors with different parameter lists. One can call another with `this(...)` to avoid repeating code.

items: `this(...)` must be the **first statement** in the constructor.
Only constructors can call `this(...)`; methods cannot.
Constructors calling each other in a cycle do not compile.

steps.prompt: What is the output?
steps.explanation: `new Box()` runs the no-arg constructor, whose first statement `this(1)` runs `Box(int)` completely (printing B1) before the rest of `Box()` prints A.

steps.prompt: Tap the line that does not compile.
steps.explanation: `this(...)` must be the very first statement of a constructor. Here a print comes first, so the call on line 5 is a compile error.

blocks.text: Add a return type and it is **no longer a constructor** — it's an ordinary method that happens to share the class name. It compiles, but `new` never calls it.

blocks.title: Legal but sneaky
blocks.text: `void ClassName()` is legal and a classic exam trick. Since no real constructor is declared, the class gets a default constructor that does nothing.

steps.prompt: What is the output?
steps.explanation: `void Robot()` has a return type, so it's a method, not a constructor. `new Robot()` uses the default constructor, and the method is never called. `id` keeps its initial value.

blocks.text: A `final` field must be assigned **exactly once**: at its declaration, in an initializer block, or in **every** constructor.

items: Not assigned on some constructor path: compile error.
Assigned twice (e.g. at declaration and in a constructor): compile error.
A constructor that starts with `this(...)` counts as assigning what the called constructor assigns.

steps.prompt: The code does not compile. Which three changes, each on its own, fix it? Choose three.
options: Change line 2 to final int id = 0;
steps.explanation: `Account()` leaves the final field `id` unassigned. Assigning it there, or delegating with `this(0)`, fixes that. Removing `final` also works because non-final fields get a default. Initializing at the declaration makes line 6 a second assignment, and assigning twice in one constructor is also an error.

steps.prompt: Build a class whose constructor stores x.
steps.explanation: A constructor has the class name and no return type. Inside it, `this.x` is the field and `x` is the parameter. `void Point(int x)` would be a method, not a constructor.

lessons.title: Initializers & init order
lessons.summary: Static and instance blocks, and the order everything runs in.

blocks.text: A bare `{ ... }` block in a class body is an **instance initializer**. It runs every time an object is created, **before the constructor body**.

items: Field initializers (`String s = "a";`) and instance blocks run **top to bottom, in source order**.
Then the constructor body runs.
Where the constructor appears in the file doesn't matter.

steps.prompt: What is the output?
steps.explanation: Field initializer and instance blocks run in source order: `s = "a"`, then `+= "b"`, then `+= "d"` (the second block, even though it is below the constructor). The constructor body runs last and adds `c`.

blocks.text: `static { ... }` runs **once**, when the class is first loaded (first used). Static field initializers and static blocks run top to bottom.

blocks.title: Main goes first
blocks.text: The class with `main` is loaded before `main` runs, so its static blocks print **before** anything in `main`.

steps.prompt: A static initializer block runs every time a new object of the class is created.
steps.explanation: A static block runs once, when the class is initialized. It is instance initializer blocks (without `static`) that run for every new object.

blocks.text: For a class without a parent class (inheritance comes in Unit 4):

rows: static fields + static blocks, top to bottom
instance fields + instance blocks, top to bottom

blocks.caption: Prints: S M I C I C

verify.value: S M I C I C

blocks.title: On the exam
blocks.text: Classic "what is printed?" questions mix static blocks, instance blocks and constructors. Work in order: static once, then per object fields/blocks, then the constructor.

steps.prompt: What is the output?
steps.explanation: Loading `Init` (before `main`) runs the static block: x becomes 6, prints `6`. Then `main` prints `main`. Each `new Init()` starts with a fresh `y = 10`, adds `x` (16), then runs the constructor. `x` is never changed again, so both objects print 16.

steps.prompt: Arrange the output lines in the order they are printed.
steps.explanation: `Shop` is loaded before `main` runs, so the static block prints first. Then `main` prints. `new Shop()` runs the instance block before the constructor body.

blocks.text: A field initializer may not **read** a field declared further down by its simple name. That's an **illegal forward reference** and does not compile.

blocks.title: Only in initializers
blocks.text: Order matters only for **reading by simple name** in initializers. Methods and constructors can use any field, wherever it's declared.

steps.prompt: Tap the line that does not compile.
steps.explanation: Line 4 reads `limit` before its declaration on line 5: an illegal forward reference. Line 3 is fine because `max` is declared above it. Line 7 is inside a method, where declaration order doesn't matter.

steps.prompt: What is the output?
steps.explanation: `Main` is initialized before `main` runs: `M`. Then `start`. `Helper` is only initialized when first used — reading `Helper.v` triggers its static block (`H`) and then the value `3` is printed.

lessons.title: Overloading & varargs
lessons.summary: Same name, different parameters, and how Java picks one.

blocks.text: **Overloading** means several methods share a name but differ in their **parameter types** (number, type or order). The compiler picks one based on the arguments.

items: Signature = method name + parameter types.
Return type, parameter **names**, `static`, and `throws` don't count.
Two methods with the same signature don't compile, even with different return types.

blocks.title: Python vs Java
blocks.text: Python has no overloading: a second `def add` simply replaces the first. Java keeps every version and chooses one **at compile time**.

steps.prompt: A class has the method below. Which two methods can be added to the same class? Choose two.
steps.code: void print(int x, String s) {}
options: int print(int a, String b) { return 0; }
static void print(int y, String t) {}
void print(int x, String s) throws Exception {}
steps.explanation: Swapping parameter order or changing the count gives a new signature. Changing only the return type, the parameter names, `static`, or the `throws` clause leaves the signature `print(int, String)` unchanged, so it's a duplicate.

blocks.text: When several overloads could accept the arguments, Java tries these steps **in order** and stops at the first that finds a match:

blocks.title: One kind of conversion
blocks.text: Java will not widen **and then** box. A `long` argument can never match `Integer`. But it can box and then widen to a reference type: `int` → `Integer` → `Object`.

steps.prompt: What is the output?
steps.explanation: `go(i)`: no `go(int)`, so widening to `long` wins before boxing. `go(Integer.valueOf(2))`: exact match for `Integer`. `go("x")`: a String only fits `Object`.

steps.prompt: What is the output?
steps.explanation: `'a'` is a `char`, which widens to `int`: first match. `3L` is a `long`; it can't narrow to `int`, so Java boxes it to `Long`, which is an `Object`.

blocks.text: `int... nums` accepts **zero or more** ints. Inside the method, `nums` is an `int[]` array (arrays are covered in Unit 6).

items: Only **one** varargs parameter per method.
It must be the **last** parameter.
You may pass an array instead of a list of values.
Varargs is the **last resort** in overload resolution.

blocks.title: T[] is not T...
blocks.text: Only a `T...` parameter accepts separate arguments. If a method declares `int[] nums`, then `f(1, 2)` doesn't compile; you must pass an array. Both forms accept `new int[]{1, 2}`.

steps.prompt: Which two method declarations compile? Choose two.
steps.explanation: A varargs parameter must be last and there can be only one. `int[]... x` is legal: a varargs of arrays. `int...` needs a parameter name.

steps.prompt: Complete the method so count("a", "b", "c") returns 3.
steps.explanation: `String...` declares varargs. Inside, `words` is a `String[]`, and arrays use the **field** `length` — not `length()` (that's for String) and not `size()` (that's for collections).

blocks.text: If two overloads match equally well, the call is **ambiguous** and does not compile.

A `null` argument fits any reference type. Java picks the **most specific** one: `String` beats `Object`, because every String is an Object. If two unrelated types both fit, like `String` and `StringBuilder`, the call is ambiguous.

Two more traps. Passing `null` to an `Object...` parameter passes a **null array**; cast it to `Object` to get a one-element array. And a wrapper argument such as `Short` matches an `Object` parameter by plain subtyping in phase 1, so it wins before unboxing and widening to `long` are even considered.

blocks.caption: Prints null array, 1 element, Object

steps.prompt: What is the output?
steps.explanation: `null` matches all three. `String` and `StringBuilder` are both more specific than `Object`, but neither is more specific than the other, so the call on line 12 is ambiguous and does not compile.

steps.prompt: What is the output?
steps.explanation: Varargs is only tried when no other overload works. `v(1, 2)` matches `v(long, long)` by widening, which is an earlier step than varargs.

lessons.title: Pass-by-value
lessons.summary: What a method can and can't change for its caller.

blocks.text: Java passes **every** argument **by value**: the method gets a copy. For a primitive, it's a copy of the number.

blocks.caption: Prints 5 — only the copy changed

blocks.text: For an object, the copied value is the **reference**. Caller and method now point to the **same object**.

items: Changing the object through the parameter (`sb.append(...)`, `s.value = 9`) **is** visible to the caller.
Reassigning the parameter (`sb = new StringBuilder()`) only changes the method's copy. The caller **doesn't** see it.

blocks.title: Python vs Java
blocks.text: Same model as Python ("pass object reference by value"). The difference: Java primitives like `int` are plain values, not objects.

steps.prompt: What is the output?
steps.explanation: `n` is a copy of the int, so the caller's `n` stays 1. `s` is a copy of the reference; both point to the same Score object, so setting `s.value` is visible.

steps.prompt: What is the output?
steps.explanation: `swap` reassigns its parameter to a new Box, then changes that new Box; the caller's box is untouched (`toy`). `fill` changes the object the caller's reference points to, so `pen` is visible.

blocks.text: `String` is **immutable**. `s + "!"`, `s.concat(...)`, `s.toUpperCase()` all return a **new** String. Inside a method, `s = s + "!"` just reassigns the local copy.

blocks.title: Ignored results
blocks.text: `s.toUpperCase();` on its own line does nothing useful: the result is thrown away. On the exam, check whether the return value is assigned.

steps.prompt: What is the output?
steps.explanation: `s = s + "!"` creates a new String and points the local `s` at it; the caller's `s` is still `hi`. `toUpperCase()`'s result is discarded. `sb.append` changes the shared StringBuilder object, so the caller sees `hi!`.

blocks.text: To give the caller a new value, **return** it — and the caller must **assign** it.

steps.prompt: A method can make the caller's variable point to a different object by assigning a new object to its parameter.
steps.explanation: The parameter is a copy of the caller's reference. Reassigning it changes only the copy. To hand back a new object, return it and let the caller assign it.

steps.prompt: Complete the code so it prints 8.
steps.explanation: A method sends a value back with `return`. The caller passes `x` (4) and assigns the result back to `x`. `n` is not visible in `main`, and `twice(8)` would print 16.

lessons.title: Scope, shadowing & var
lessons.summary: Where variables live, this.x = x, and var's rules.

rows: its declaration → end of its block { }

blocks.caption: Prints 5

steps.prompt: Tap the line that does not compile.
steps.explanation: `bonus` is declared inside the `if` block, so its scope ends at the closing brace on line 11. Line 12 can't see it.

blocks.text: A local variable or parameter with the same name as a field **shadows** (hides) the field. Use `this.name` to reach the field.

blocks.title: Self-assignment
blocks.text: `speed = speed;` compiles but assigns the parameter to itself. The field is unchanged.
Inside one method, you **can't** declare a local with the same name as another local or parameter still in scope.

steps.prompt: What is the output?
steps.explanation: In `set`, `speed = speed` assigns the parameter to itself; the field stays 10. `boost` uses `this.speed`, so the field becomes 10 + 5 = 15.

steps.prompt: This code compiles.
steps.explanation: A local variable can shadow a **field**, but not another **local** that is still in scope. The outer `x` is in scope inside the loop, so redeclaring `x` on line 3 is an error.

blocks.text: `var` declares a **local** variable whose type is inferred from the initializer. The type is fixed at compile time; `var` is not dynamic typing.

items: Only for **local variables** (including `for` loops). Not fields, parameters or return types.
Needs an initializer in the same statement: `var x;` fails.
Can't be initialized to `null` or to an array initializer `{1, 2}`.
One variable per statement: `var a = 1, b = 2;` fails.
Also allowed for lambda parameters (Unit 7).

blocks.title: Python vs Java
blocks.text: Python variables can change type at any time. `var n = 10;` makes `n` an `int` forever; assigning a String later is a compile error.

blocks.title: No brackets on var
blocks.text: `var` can't carry array brackets: `var[] a` and `var a[]` don't compile. Put the brackets on the right: `var a = new int[3];`.

blocks.code:
var ok = new int[3];
var bad[] = new int[3];
blocks.caption: Line 2 does not compile

steps.prompt: Which three lines compile inside a method? Choose three.
steps.explanation: `var` needs an initializer with a real type: not missing, not `null`, not a bare array initializer. `var` is a **reserved type name**, not a keyword, so a variable may be called `var` — but a class may not.

steps.prompt: Tap the line that does not compile.
steps.explanation: `var total = 0;` makes `total` an `int` for good. Assigning a String on line 8 is a type mismatch. `var` in a `for` loop (line 5) is allowed.

steps.prompt: What is the output?
steps.explanation: `x` is inferred as `int` and `y` as `double`. `x / 2` is integer division: 2. Then `2 + 2.0` is the double 4.0, so `z` is a `double`.

lessons.title: Access, encapsulation & immutability
lessons.summary: private/public, getters, and building immutable classes.

blocks.text: Classes live in **packages** (`package com.shop;` as the first line). Access modifiers control who can see a member.

blocks.title: No keyword
blocks.text: From most to least restrictive: private → package → protected → public. "Package access" has no keyword; writing `package` before a member does not compile.

`protected` from **another package** is narrower than it looks. A subclass may use an inherited protected member only through `this`, `super`, or a reference of its **own** type (or a subtype). Through a reference typed as the parent, it doesn't compile.

blocks.caption: Gadget and Item are in different packages

steps.prompt: Which access level makes a member visible only to classes in the same package?
steps.explanation: Leaving out the modifier gives package access. `protected` is wider: it adds subclasses in other packages. `private` limits access to the class itself.

blocks.text: **Encapsulation**: keep fields `private` and expose behaviour through methods. The class can then validate every change.

blocks.title: Python vs Java
blocks.text: Python's `_balance` is only a naming convention. Java's `private` is enforced by the compiler: other classes simply can't compile code that touches it.

steps.prompt: Tap the line that does not compile.
steps.explanation: `cash` is private to `Wallet`, so `Main` can't read it directly (line 11). The package-access getter on line 10 is fine.

steps.prompt: This code compiles.
steps.explanation: `private` is per **class**, not per object. Code inside `Wallet` may read the private field of **any** Wallet, including the `other` parameter.

items: Make the class `final` (no subclass can add mutation).
Make every field `private final`.
No setters. Set everything in the constructor.
For mutable inputs (List, StringBuilder, arrays), store a **copy** in the constructor…
…and return a **copy** (or unmodifiable view) from getters.

blocks.caption: String is already immutable, so no copy needed

blocks.title: final ≠ immutable
blocks.text: `final` on a field freezes the **reference**, not the object. A `private final List` can still be changed by anyone holding the same list.

steps.prompt: What is the output?
options: An exception is thrown at runtime
steps.explanation: The constructor stores the caller's list itself, and the getter hands out that same list. So `src.add("Bob")` and `r.names().add("Cy")` both change the Roster's list: 3 elements. `final` only stops reassigning the field.

steps.prompt: Using the Roster class from the last question: which two changes are both needed so no caller can ever change a Roster's list? Choose two.
options: Copy the list in the constructor: new ArrayList<>(names)
Return a copy from names(): new ArrayList<>(names)
steps.explanation: The list can leak in two directions: the caller keeps a reference to the list passed in, and the getter hands out the internal list. A defensive copy is needed at **both** points. `final` on a method only stops overriding.

steps.prompt: Make Money immutable.
steps.explanation: A `final` class can't be subclassed, and a `private final` field can be set only once, in the constructor. Top-level classes can't be `static`, and `abstract` would forbid creating objects.

lessons.title: Records
lessons.summary: Compact data classes: components, accessors and constructors.

steps.title: A data class in one line

blocks.text: A **record** declares its data in a header. The compiler generates the rest.

blocks.caption: Prints Point[x=1, y=2], 3, true

items: A `private final` field per component.
A **canonical constructor** taking all components in order.
Accessor methods named **exactly like the components**: `x()`, not `getX()`.
`equals()`, `hashCode()` and `toString()` based on the components.

blocks.title: Python vs Java
blocks.text: Like `@dataclass(frozen=True)`. But you read data by calling methods: `p.x()`, not `p.x`.

steps.prompt: What is the output?
steps.explanation: A record's `toString()` prints the record name, then each component as `name=value` inside square brackets, separated by `, `. `title()` is the generated accessor.

steps.prompt: Tap the line that does not compile.
steps.explanation: Record accessors use the component name: `age()`. No `getAge()` method is generated.

blocks.text: To validate or normalize, write a **compact constructor**: the record name with **no parameter list**. The fields are assigned automatically **after** its body runs.

items: You may reassign the **parameters** (`value = ...`). The changed value is what gets stored.
You may **not** assign the fields (`this.value = ...`): compile error.

blocks.title: No parentheses
blocks.text: A compact constructor looks like an instance initializer with a name in front. No parentheses — `Name() { }` would be a different, non-canonical constructor.

blocks.title: No throws clause
blocks.text: A canonical or compact constructor can't declare `throws`. It may still throw unchecked exceptions such as `IllegalArgumentException`.

blocks.caption: Line 2 does not compile

steps.prompt: What is the output?
steps.explanation: The compact constructor replaces a negative parameter with 0 before the field is assigned, so the first record stores 0. The second stores 7 unchanged.

steps.prompt: Tap the line that does not compile.
steps.explanation: In a compact constructor you may reassign the parameter (line 3), but you may not assign the field. The compiler assigns `this.text` itself after the body.

blocks.text: You can also write the **long canonical form** with all parameters; then you must assign every field yourself. Any **other** constructor must start by calling `this(...)`.

steps.prompt: This code compiles.
steps.explanation: `Pair(String a)` is not the canonical constructor, so its first statement must be `this(...)` — for example `this(a, "")`. Assigning fields directly is not allowed there.

steps.title: What records can and can't do

items: Every record implicitly extends `java.lang.Record`.
A record nested in a class is implicitly `static`.
Fields are `final`, but a component like a `List` can still be changed from outside — copy it for real immutability.

blocks.text: The generated `equals` compares each component with `Objects.equals`, so an **array** component compares by reference. The generated `toString`, `equals` and `hashCode` read the **fields** directly, so overriding an accessor doesn't change them.

blocks.caption: Prints X Tag[name=x], then false

steps.prompt: Which two records compile? Choose two.
steps.explanation: Static fields are fine, and records can implement interfaces. Records can't declare extra instance fields, can't use `extends`, and a compact constructor can't assign fields.

steps.prompt: What is the output?
steps.explanation: Two `new` calls create two objects, so `==` is false. The generated `equals()` compares components, and `hashCode()` is consistent with it, so both are true.

steps.prompt: Which two statements are true? Choose two.
options: A static method called through a null reference of its class does not throw an exception.
A static method can read instance fields directly.
A static initializer block runs once per class.
Each object gets its own copy of a static field.
steps.explanation: Static calls are resolved by the declared type, so a null reference is never used. Static blocks run once when the class is initialized. Static fields are shared, static methods have no instance, and the syntax is `import static`.

steps.prompt: Which statement compiles when placed inside a method?
steps.explanation: `var c = new ArrayList<>();` compiles; with nothing to infer from, the type is `ArrayList<Object>`. `var` can't be `null`, can't use a bare array initializer, and can't declare several variables.

steps.prompt: Which two are part of the recipe for an immutable class? Choose two.
options: The class has a public no-arg constructor
Mutable fields are copied when received and when returned
Every field has a setter that checks its input
steps.explanation: An immutable class has private final fields set once in the constructor, no setters, defensive copies for mutable data, and is usually `final`. A no-arg constructor or static methods have nothing to do with it.
